content:
Dozens of presidential briefing documents were declassified on Friday, coinciding with the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detailing the intelligence gathered by government officials about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and transformed America's national security landscape.

The documents show how security analysts tracked bin Laden's movements and support network, as well as concerns about potential threats to U.S. targets. The files also detail officials' understanding of his networks in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were funded.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe called the release an "extraordinary act of transparency," saying the declassification represents the largest batch of President's Daily Briefs ever released by the agency — these highly classified briefings prepared by the intelligence community for the government's top leadership.

The documents span a wide range, going back as far as a February 1998 file prepared for then-President Bill Clinton titled "Terrorists Seek to Acquire Weapons of Mass Destruction," which mentioned bin Laden and other Islamic extremists; the most recent is a September 12, 2001 report, in which a source said the attacks had been planned for two years and had at one point targeted the U.S. Capitol.

An April 1998 document described the Taliban's reluctance to hand over bin Laden, noting that he was considered a "guest" in Afghanistan and that the Taliban "grateful for the assistance he provided during the Soviet occupation," making them "unwilling to monitor or restrict his activities."

In July 1998, briefers assessed that "bin Laden is likely to have made attacking U.S. interests inside the United States a high priority," and noted his "interest in using chemical and biological weapons to launch attacks."

Two months later, a briefer wrote that bin Laden's "first preference was to attack Washington, D.C., on the U.S. homeland," and that al-Qaeda "could fly an aircraft loaded with explosives into a U.S. city."

Potential hijacking operations were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described planners "had evaded security in a test run at an unpublicized airport in New York," and that "some members of bin Laden's network had received hijacking training."

Other documents detailed bin Laden's efforts to obtain materials for a "dirty bomb" — a conventional weapon laced with radioactive material. Intelligence officials said that as of June 1999, his operatives had conducted experiments on explosives to "increase the yield of their output."

About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials knew that bin Laden appeared to be concealing from the Taliban his willingness to launch unprovoked attacks against the United States. Briefings prepared for President George W. Bush in early 2001 focused in part on bin Laden's "crude efforts to experiment with production and deployment of biological weapons."

A report one month before the attacks stated that bin Laden was "committed to staging a terrorist attack on the U.S. homeland," and noted that al-Qaeda's 1998 attacks on U.S. embassies "showed he would plan operations years in advance and not be deterred by setbacks."

At the time — August 2001 — officials wrote that "there had been suspicious activity in the United States consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York," and added that the FBI "was conducting approximately 70 full-field investigations across the country that it believed were related to bin Laden."

Many of the documents are redacted to conceal source names and other identifying information. The batch does not appear to yield any breakthroughs regarding the planning of the attacks or U.S. officials' understanding of how events unfolded.

In the years after the attacks, a bipartisan commission specifically pointed to insufficient information-sharing between agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and made a number of recommendations that led to the creation of new positions, including a centralized Director of National Intelligence and the National Counterterrorism Center, responsible for analyzing counterterrorism intelligence from different government agencies both at home and abroad.

When asked about its response to the declassified documents, the White House pointed to the fact that the National Archives also declassified another batch of documents on Friday. That batch includes interview transcripts with national security officials from the Clinton and Bush administrations, produced by the commission that investigated the attacks between 2002 and 2004.
